items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: I made many, many records with Billie Holiday and it was always a joy just to be in her company

ctx.x: Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. Regardless what he played when he was there, you miss

seeing him. He had an aura about him that everybody loved. Everybody loved Count Basie. Everybody loved Duke Ellington. The big bands were so popular in those days, until, and they, most of the musicians in those days demanded respect because they were an artist. And they were all individualists. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. She’s the only one sounded like that. If Louis…
I guess it’s a tribute of a sort.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We had a manager named Maceo Birch, he travelled with the band, and Billie Holiday travelled with the band for a while when she first joined the band.

ctx.x: Who travelled with the band other than the band members?
We had a manager named Maceo Birch, he travelled with the band, and Billie Holiday travelled with the band for a while when she first joined the band. Then, Jimmy Rushing he travelled with the band.
Did you have any band boys to help out?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: And then -- because after Billie Holiday left, we didn't want any singer anyway, you know.

ctx.x: Sure. Sure. And then -- because after Billie Holiday left, we didn't want any singer anyway, you know.
I heard her with the band.
